title: Polydorus. Delos
titleEn: The Voice from the Mound and the Oracle at Delos — Aeneid III.1–98
part: The Voice from the Mound and the Oracle at Delos (III.1–98)
about: Aeneas, still telling Dido his story, takes up the tale after Troy's fall. The gods have resolved to overthrow Asia's power and Priam's undeserving people, and the survivors are driven by omens to seek distant exile. They build a fleet at the foot of Antandros under Phrygian Ida, uncertain where the fates will let them settle, and at the start of summer Anchises bids them sail; Aeneas leaves his country in tears with his companions, his son, the Penates and the great gods. They come to Thrace, a land of Mars once ruled by fierce Lycurgus and an old friend of Troy, and Aeneas begins to lay out walls and names the settlement from his own name. While sacrificing to Venus and the gods who bless new undertakings, and to Jupiter, he tries to tear leafy shoots from a mound to cover the altars; the shoots bleed. He is chilled with fear, tries a second, and then a third, and a groan comes from deep in the mound: it is Polydorus, Priam's son, buried there under a harvest of spears grown from the weapons that killed him, who tells Aeneas to flee that cruel and greedy shore. Aeneas explains the background: Priam had secretly sent the boy with a great weight of gold to the Thracian king, who, once Troy's fortunes failed, sided with Agamemnon's victors, broke every law of right and killed his guest for the gold. After consulting Anchises and the chiefs, the Trojans resolve to leave that defiled land; they first give Polydorus a full funeral, with an altar to the Manes, dark fillets, cypress, loosed-haired Trojan women, bowls of milk and sacred blood, and a last cry over the tomb. When the sea is calm and the south wind rises, they sail to Delos, the holy island that Apollo moored fast to Myconos and Gyaros so that it no longer drifted. King Anius, king and priest in one, greets Anchises as an old friend. Aeneas prays in the old temple for a home of their own, for walls and a lasting city, for the survivors of the Greeks and fierce Achilles, and for a sign; the place shakes, the laurels and the mountain tremble, the tripod bellows, and a voice bids the hardy Dardanids to seek the ancient mother that first bore them: there the house of Aeneas will rule every shore, and his children's children after them.

sentences.t:
Postquam res Asiae Priamique evertere gentem
immeritam visum Superis, ceciditque superbum
Ilium, et omnis humo fumat Neptunia Troia,
sentences.l:
After the fortunes of Asia and Priam's nation to overturn,
undeserving, it seemed good to the Powers above, and fell the proud
Ilium, and all smokes from the ground, Neptune's Troy,
sentences.i: When the powers above had resolved to bring down the might of Asia and Priam's people, who had not deserved it, and proud Ilium had fallen, and all of Neptune's Troy lay smoking from the ground,
sentences.n: Aeneas, still telling his story to Dido, begins Book III with the fall of Troy already behind him. 'visum' is the perfect passive participle of 'video' used impersonally with 'est' left out, 'it seemed good, was resolved', and 'Superis' (the gods above) is a dative of the person to whom it seemed so; 'evertere' is an infinitive that serves as the subject of 'visum'. 'res Asiae' is 'the power, the state of Asia' ('res' is a wide word, 'affairs, fortune'); 'immeritam' agrees with 'gentem', 'undeserving' of its fate. 'ceciditque' is the perfect of 'cado'. 'omnis… Troia' is nominative singular feminine, 'all Troy'; 'humo' is an ablative of the place from which, 'from the ground'. 'Neptunia' recalls the legend that Neptune built the walls of Troy.

sentences.t:
diversa exsilia et desertas quaerere terras
auguriis agimur divom,
sentences.l:
scattered exiles and deserted lands to seek
by omens we are driven of the gods,
sentences.i: we are driven by the omens of the gods to seek far-scattered places of exile and empty lands,
sentences.n: 'agimur' is the present passive of 'ago', 'we are driven'; 'quaerere' is an infinitive of purpose after it, a poetic construction in Latin where prose would use a subjunctive clause. 'diversa exsilia' is 'exiles in different directions, widely scattered', that is, places of exile; 'desertas… terras' are 'empty, abandoned lands'. 'auguriis… divom' is an ablative of means or cause. 'divom' is the old genitive plural in -om for 'divorum', the form that Greenough prints (you'll see this constantly; the Latin Library prints 'diuum', only a different spelling).

sentences.t:
classemque sub ipsa
Antandro et Phrygiae molimur montibus Idae,
incerti, quo fata ferant, ubi sistere detur,
sentences.l:
and a fleet right beneath
Antandros and under Phrygian Ida's mountains we build,
uncertain whither the fates may carry, where to settle it be granted,
sentences.i: and we build a fleet at the foot of Antandros itself, below the mountains of Phrygian Ida, not knowing where the fates may bear us or where we shall be allowed to settle,
sentences.n: 'Antandro' is the ablative of Antandros, a port in the Troad at the foot of Mount Ida, and 'ipsa' agrees with it, 'right under Antandros itself'; 'sub' governs both 'Antandro' and 'montibus… Idae'. 'Phrygiae' means 'Trojan' here: the Ida behind Troy, not the Cretan one. 'molimur' is the present of the deponent 'molior', 'toil at, build'. 'incerti' is nominative plural, agreeing with the 'we' of the verb. 'quo fata ferant' and 'ubi sistere detur' are indirect questions, so the verbs are subjunctive: 'ferant' is present subjunctive of 'fero', and 'detur' is the impersonal present passive subjunctive of 'do', 'where it may be granted to settle', with 'sistere' as its infinitive.

sentences.t: contrahimusque viros.
sentences.l: and we draw together men.
sentences.i: and we muster men.
sentences.n: 'contrahimus' is 'draw together, assemble'; '-que' joins it to the other presents. The three present-tense verbs of the sentence ('agimur', 'molimur', 'contrahimus') are the narrative present that Aeneas uses for the preparations. 'viros' is an accusative plural, 'men'. The period closes a sentence that began in line 1.

sentences.t:
Vix prima inceperat aestas,
et pater Anchises dare fatis vela iubebat;
sentences.l:
Scarcely had the first summer begun,
and father Anchises to give to the fates sails was bidding;
sentences.i: Summer had hardly begun when my father Anchises was bidding us give our sails to the fates;
sentences.n: 'inceperat' is the pluperfect of 'incipio'; 'prima aestas' is early summer. 'et' after 'vix' stands where Latin would otherwise use 'cum', 'when': the second event arrives as a simple addition (you'll see this pattern of an inverted clause constantly). 'dare fatis vela' is a vivid phrase, 'give sails to the fates', that is, 'set sail and trust to fate'. 'iubebat' is an imperfect, 'was bidding', and takes an accusative and infinitive; the accusative 'nos' is understood. 'Anchises' is the Greek nominative; Anchises is Aeneas' aged father.

sentences.t:
litora cum patriae lacrimans portusque relinquo
et campos, ubi Troia fuit:
sentences.l:
when the shores of the fatherland, weeping, and the harbours I leave
and the plains, where Troy was:
sentences.i: when I leave, in tears, my country's coast, her harbours, and the open ground where Troy had stood:
sentences.n: 'cum' with the indicative 'relinquo' is the inverted 'cum' ('when'): the main action is given in the 'cum' clause, while 'vix… iubebat' in the line before gives the setting. 'lacrimans' is a present participle, 'weeping', agreeing with the 'I' of 'relinquo'. 'patriae' is a genitive, 'of my fatherland', with 'litora'; the three objects are 'litora' (shores), 'portus' (joined to it by '-que') and 'campos' (added by 'et'). 'ubi Troia fuit' is 'where Troy was': the perfect 'fuit' means that Troy is no more. The colon prepares the second half of the sentence.

sentences.t:
feror exsul in altum
cum sociis natoque Penatibus et magnis dis.
sentences.l:
I am borne an exile into the deep
with companions and son, the Penates and the great gods.
sentences.i: and I am carried out, an exile, onto the open sea with my comrades, my son, the household gods, and the great gods.
sentences.n: 'feror' is the present passive of 'fero', 'I am carried', in the sense 'I put out'; 'exsul' is a nominative in apposition to the subject, 'as an exile'; 'in altum' is 'into the deep, out to sea'. Here 'cum' is a preposition (not a conjunction as in the line before) and governs the ablatives 'sociis', 'natoque' (with '-que', 'and with my son'), 'Penatibus', and 'dis'. 'dis' is a contracted ablative plural of 'deus' (for 'deis'). The Penates are Troy's household gods, whom Aeneas brings out of the city; 'magnis dis', 'the great gods', is added without explanation, and who exactly is meant is not settled here.

sentences.t:
Terra procul vastis colitur Mavortia campis,
Thraces arant, acri quondam regnata Lycurgo,
hospitium antiquum Troiae sociique Penates,
sentences.l:
A land far off with wide plains is tilled, Mavortian,
Thracians plough it, once ruled by fierce Lycurgus,
a guest-friendship ancient with Troy, and allied Penates,
sentences.i: Far off lies a land of broad plains, the country of Mars, which Thracians plough, once ruled by fierce Lycurgus, an old friend of Troy, its gods allied to ours,
sentences.n: A new paragraph, a new scene: the first landing, in Thrace. 'colitur' is the present passive of 'colo', 'is tilled, is inhabited'. 'Mavortia' is an adjective from 'Mavors', the old form of 'Mars', and Thrace was the land of Mars. 'vastis… campis' is an ablative, 'with wide plains' (of quality or of place). 'Thraces' is the nominative plural of 'Thrax', 'Thracians'; 'arant' is 'plough'. 'regnata' is a perfect passive participle of the intransitive 'regno', 'ruled', used as a passive in verse, with 'Lycurgo' an ablative of the agent without a preposition. Lycurgus, in the old tale, was the Thracian king who opposed Dionysus. 'hospitium antiquum Troiae sociique Penates' is in apposition to 'terra': the land is 'an old guest-friendship with Troy', and 'sociique Penates' is 'and allied household gods', best taken as the land's own gods, friendly to Troy's.

sentences.t: dum Fortuna fuit.
sentences.l: while Fortune was.
sentences.i: so long as our fortune lasted.
sentences.n: 'dum' means 'as long as' and takes the indicative, here the perfect 'fuit'. 'Fortuna fuit' is 'Fortune was', that is, Troy's good fortune lasted: the sentence says that the friendship dates from the time of Troy's prosperity, and the perfect again looks back on something that is over.

sentences.t:
Feror huc, et litore curvo
moenia prima loco, fatis ingressus iniquis,
Aeneadasque meo nomen de nomine fingo.
sentences.l:
I am borne here, and on a curved shore
the first walls I place, having entered upon fates unkind,
and Aeneadae, from my own name, the name I fashion.
sentences.i: I come here, and on the curving shore I mark out the first walls of a city, setting out under unkind fates, and I give the people a name drawn from my own, calling them Aeneadae.
sentences.n: 'feror' is the passive of 'fero' ('I am carried'), as at line 11. 'loco' in 'moenia prima loco' is the first person singular present of the verb 'loco', 'I place, set down', not the noun: 'I lay down the first walls'; 'litore curvo' is an ablative of place. 'ingressus' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'ingredior', 'having set out upon (the work)', and 'fatis… iniquis' is an ablative of attendant circumstances, 'under unkind fates': the beginning is ill-starred. 'Aeneadas… nomen fingo' is 'I fashion the name Aeneadae': 'Aeneadas' is an accusative plural of a Greek-style patronymic, 'sons of Aeneas', and 'meo… de nomine' is 'from my own name'.

sentences.t:
Sacra Dionaeae matri divisque ferebam
auspicibus coeptorum operum, superoque nitentem
caelicolum regi mactabam in litore taurum.
sentences.l:
Offerings to Dionaean mother and to the gods,
sponsors of the works begun, I was bringing, and to the high
king of the heaven-dwellers I was slaying on the shore a shining bull.
sentences.i: I was offering sacrifice to my mother, Dione's daughter, and to the gods who favour undertakings newly begun, and on the shore I was slaughtering a gleaming bull for the high king of the heaven-dwellers.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Sacra… ferebam' is 'I was bringing sacred offerings', that is, 'I was sacrificing'. 'Dionaeae matri' is Venus, called 'Dionaea' from her mother Dione in the Greek tradition; the dative goes with 'ferebam'. 'divis… auspicibus coeptorum operum' is 'to the gods, sponsors of the works begun', with 'coeptorum operum' a genitive. 'superoque… caelicolum regi' is 'to the high king of the heaven-dwellers', Jupiter, and 'supero' agrees with 'regi'; 'caelicolum' is the old genitive plural in -um for 'caelicolarum'. 'nitentem' is 'shining, sleek', with 'taurum'. 'mactabam' is the imperfect, 'was slaying (as a sacrifice)'.

sentences.t:
Forte fuit iuxta tumulus, quo cornea summo
virgulta et densis hastilibus horrida myrtus.
sentences.l:
By chance there was near a mound, on whose top cornel
shrubs and, bristling with thick spear-shafts, myrtle.
sentences.i: By chance there was a mound close by, and on its crest grew cornel saplings and a myrtle bristling with thick spear-shafts.
sentences.n: 'Forte' is an ablative of 'fors' used as an adverb, 'by chance'; 'iuxta' is an adverb, 'close by'. 'quo… summo' is a relative with an ablative of place, 'on whose top', and a verb ('there were') is left out. 'cornea virgulta' are 'cornel-wood saplings' (neuter plural), 'myrtus' is a feminine noun in the nominative, and 'densis hastilibus horrida' is 'bristling with dense spear-shafts', the straight shoots of the myrtle. The picture prepares for the spears of lines 45-46.

sentences.t:
Accessi, viridemque ab humo convellere silvam
conatus, ramis tegerem ut frondentibus aras,
horrendum et dictu video mirabile monstrum.
sentences.l:
I approached, and the green wood from the ground to tear up
having tried, so that with branches I might cover leafy the altars,
a dreadful portent, and wonderful to tell, I see.
sentences.i: I went up and tried to wrench a green growth from the soil, so that I might cover the altars with leafy boughs; and I see a portent, dreadful and amazing to tell.
sentences.n: 'conatus' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'conor', 'having tried', with the infinitive 'convellere'. 'viridem… silvam' is 'green wood', a singular for the leafy branches; 'ab humo' is 'from the ground'. 'tegerem ut' is 'ut tegerem' with the word order inverted: a purpose clause, with 'tegerem' the imperfect subjunctive after the past 'accessi', and 'ramis… frondentibus' an ablative of means. 'horrendum et… mirabile' goes with 'monstrum': 'horrendum' is a gerundive used as an adjective, 'to be shuddered at'; 'dictu' is a supine in -u, 'in the telling', so 'mirabile dictu' is 'wonderful to tell'. 'monstrum' is a 'portent', from 'moneo'.

sentences.t:
Nam, quae prima solo ruptis radicibus arbos
vellitur, huic atro liquuntur sanguine guttae,
et terram tabo maculant.
sentences.l:
For, which first from the soil with roots broken tree
is torn up, to it with black blood run drops,
and the earth with gore they stain.
sentences.i: For from the first sapling that is torn from the soil with its roots snapped, drops flow, dark with blood, and spatter the ground with gore.
sentences.n: The relative clause 'quae prima… arbos vellitur' stands before its pronoun 'huic' ('to this one'): 'for the tree that is first torn up, from it…'. 'arbos' is the archaic nominative of 'arbor'. 'solo' is an ablative of separation and 'ruptis radicibus' an ablative absolute, 'roots broken'. 'huic' is a dative of reference, 'for it, from it'. 'liquuntur' is the third person plural present of the deponent 'liquor', 'flow, run'. 'atro… sanguine' is an ablative of means or manner with 'liquuntur', 'drops run with black blood'. 'tabo' is the ablative of 'tabum', 'gore, corrupt matter', and 'maculant' has 'guttae' as its subject, 'stain' the ground.

sentences.t:
Mihi frigidus horror
membra quatit, gelidusque coit formidine sanguis.
sentences.l:
To me a cold shudder
shakes the limbs, and chill congeals with fear the blood.
sentences.i: A cold shudder shakes my limbs, and my blood runs icy and thickens with fear.
sentences.n: 'Mihi… membra' is a dative of the person affected, close to a possessive ('the limbs to me', for 'mea membra'). 'horror' is 'a shudder' (from 'horreo', 'bristle'). 'quatit' is the present of 'quatio', 'shake'. 'coit' is the present of 'coeo', 'comes together, congeals'; 'formidine' is an ablative of cause. 'gelidus' is 'chill, icy', agreeing with 'sanguis'.

sentences.t:
Rursus et alterius lentum convellere vimen
insequor, et causas penitus temptare latentis:
sentences.l:
Again also of a second the pliant to tear up shoot
I go on, and the causes deeply to probe, lying hidden:
sentences.i: Again I press on to wrench up the pliant shoot of a second tree, and to probe to the root the causes that lie hidden:
sentences.n: 'alterius' is the genitive of 'alter', agreeing with a noun left to be understood ('of the second tree'). 'lentum… vimen' is 'the pliant shoot'. 'insequor' is 'I follow up, press on', and takes the infinitives 'convellere' and 'temptare' (a poetic construction). 'causas… latentis' has 'latentis' as an accusative plural of the present participle of 'lateo', 'lying hidden', in -is (you'll see this ending constantly, as in 'omnis', 'agrestis'). 'penitus' is 'deep within, thoroughly'. The colon leads to the second result.

sentences.t: ater et alterius sequitur de cortice sanguis.
sentences.l: black from a second's bark follows blood.
sentences.i: dark blood follows from the bark of the second as well.
sentences.n: 'et' here means 'also', and 'alterius' is again the genitive with a tree understood, 'of the second (tree)', now going with 'cortice', 'the bark'. 'ater' is 'dark, dull black', and 'sequitur' is 'follows' the pulling. The repetition shows that the first portent was no accident.

sentences.t:
Multa movens animo nymphas venerabar agrestis
Gradivumque patrem, Geticis qui praesidet arvis,
rite secundarent visus omenque levarent.
sentences.l:
Many things turning over in mind, the nymphs I was worshipping, rustic,
and Gradivus the father, who presides over the Getic fields,
that duly they would favour the sights and the omen lighten.
sentences.i: Turning many thoughts over in my mind, I began to pray to the nymphs of the countryside and to father Gradivus, who watches over the Getic fields, that they would turn the vision to good and lighten the omen.
sentences.n: 'Multa movens animo' is 'turning many things in my mind', 'animo' an ablative of place. 'venerabar' is the imperfect of the deponent 'veneror', 'I was worshipping, praying to'. 'nymphas… agrestis' has an accusative plural in -is. 'Gradivus' is a title of Mars (traditionally connected with 'gradior', 'march'), and 'Geticis… arvis' are the fields of the Getae, a Thracian people: Mars is the guardian of the land. 'rite secundarent visus omenque levarent' gives the content of the prayer: 'secundarent' and 'levarent' are imperfect subjunctives, a request without 'ut' (an indirect command). 'secundo' means 'make favourable', 'visus' is an accusative plural of the fourth declension, 'sights, visions'. 'omen' is the portent, and 'levarent' is 'lighten, relieve' it.

sentences.t:
Tertia sed postquam maiore hastilia nisu
adgredior, genibusque adversae obluctor harenae—
sentences.l:
A third, but after with greater effort the shafts
I attack, and with my knees against the opposing sand I struggle—
sentences.i: But when, with a greater effort, I set about the third shaft, and strain with my knees against the resisting sand—
sentences.n: 'sed postquam' is 'but when', with the present 'adgredior' (the narrative present). 'Tertia… hastilia' is 'the third shaft or shoot', in a poetic plural; 'maiore… nisu' is an ablative of manner, 'with greater effort'. 'adgredior' is the deponent 'aggredior', 'attack, set about' (Greenough prints 'adgr-'). 'obluctor' is the deponent 'obluctor', 'struggle against', and takes the dative 'adversae harenae'; 'genibus' is an ablative of means. The dash opens a parenthesis: Aeneas breaks off and speaks to his hearers before telling what he heard.

sentences.t: eloquar, an sileam?—
sentences.l: Shall I tell, or keep silent?—
sentences.i: Shall I tell it, or keep silent?—
sentences.n: A parenthesis addressed to his hearers: Aeneas hesitates to say what happened. 'eloquar' and 'sileam' are deliberative questions, 'am I to speak or be silent?', both present subjunctive (the first-person form 'eloquar' is the same as a future indicative, but the question is deliberative). 'an' introduces the second half of an alternative question. The second dash closes the parenthesis, and the sentence resumes with 'gemitus'.

sentences.t:
gemitus lacrimabilis imo
auditur tumulo, et vox reddita fertur ad auris:
sentences.l:
a groan, tearful, from the lowest
mound is heard, and a voice sent back is borne to my ears:
sentences.i: a pitiable groan is heard from deep inside the mound, and a voice comes back to my ears:
sentences.n: 'gemitus lacrimabilis' is 'a groan to be wept over, a pitiable groan'. 'imo… tumulo' is an ablative of the place from which, without a preposition, and 'imo' means 'the lowest part of', 'from the depth of the mound'. 'auditur' is the present passive of 'audio'. 'vox reddita fertur ad auris' is 'a voice, given back, is carried to the ears': 'reddita' (perfect passive participle of 'reddo') is 'given back, uttered'; 'auris' is an accusative plural in -is. The colon introduces the speech that begins in the next line.

sentences.t: “Quid miserum, Aenea, laceras?
sentences.l: “Why a wretched man, Aeneas, do you tear?
sentences.i: “Why do you tear at a wretched man, Aeneas?
sentences.n: The ghost's speech begins, with the opening “; the speaker is not yet named. 'Quid' is an accusative used as an adverb, 'why?'. 'miserum' is the masculine accusative of 'miser', 'a wretched man', the object of 'laceras', 'tear, mangle'. 'Aenea' is the vocative of 'Aeneas' (the Greek-style first declension).

sentences.t: Iam parce sepulto;
sentences.l: Now spare the buried;
sentences.i: Spare him who lies buried now;
sentences.n: 'parce' is the imperative of 'parco', which takes a dative, here 'sepulto', the perfect participle of 'sepelio' used as a noun, 'to the buried one'. 'iam' is 'now (at last)'.

sentences.t: parce pias scelerare manus.
sentences.l: spare your pious hands to defile.
sentences.i: Spare your dutiful hands the stain of guilt.
sentences.n: 'parce' takes the infinitive 'scelerare' here, 'refrain from defiling' (a poetic use). 'scelerare' is the infinitive of 'scelero', 'pollute with crime'. 'pias manus' is 'your dutiful hands': the epithet is pointed, since Aeneas is the man of 'pietas' and these are the hands that should not be stained. 'manus' is an accusative plural of the fourth declension.

sentences.t:
Non me tibi Troia
externum tulit, aut cruor hic de stipite manat.
sentences.l:
Not me to you Troy
as an outsider bore, nor blood this from the trunk flows.
sentences.i: Troy did not bear me a stranger to you, and this blood does not flow from a mere tree-trunk.
sentences.n: 'Non… tulit' is the perfect of 'fero', 'bore, brought forth'. 'externum' is a predicative accusative, 'as an outsider', with 'tibi' a dative of reference, 'to you'. 'aut' after the negative has the force of 'nor'. 'cruor' is 'blood (that flows)', and 'de stipite' is 'from a trunk, a stock', 'manat' is 'flows'. The ghost insists that he is not a stranger but a Trojan.

sentences.t: Heu, fuge crudelis terras, fuge litus avarum:
sentences.l: Alas, flee cruel lands, flee the shore greedy:
sentences.i: Alas, escape these cruel lands, leave this grasping shore:
sentences.n: 'Heu' is an interjection of grief. 'fuge' is an imperative, repeated (anaphora). 'crudelis' is an accusative plural in -is, agreeing with 'terras'. 'avarum' is 'greedy', and looks ahead to the gold for which Polydorus was killed. The colon announces the explanation.

sentences.t: nam Polydorus ego;
sentences.l: for Polydorus I (am);
sentences.i: for I am Polydorus;
sentences.n: The verb 'sum' is left out ('Polydorus ego'). The name comes late and gives the speech its force. Polydorus is a young son of Priam. In the Iliad he is killed by Achilles; Virgil follows the other tradition, familiar from Euripides' Hecuba, in which a Thracian king kills him for his gold.

sentences.t:
hic confixum ferrea texit
telorum seges et iaculis increvit acutis.”
sentences.l:
here pierced covered (me) iron
of weapons harvest, and with sharp javelins grew up.”
sentences.i: here a crop of iron weapons covered me, pierced through as I was, and grew up in sharp javelins.”
sentences.n: 'hic' is an adverb, 'here'. 'confixum' is the perfect participle of 'configo', 'pierced through', and agrees with 'me' understood as the object of 'texit'. 'ferrea… seges telorum' is 'an iron crop of weapons': the weapons that killed him have taken root and sprung up as a stand of shoots, like corn. 'texit' is the perfect of 'tego', 'covered'; 'increvit' is the perfect of 'incresco', 'grew up'; 'iaculis… acutis' is an ablative of means, 'sharp' agreeing with 'javelins'. The closing ” ends Polydorus' speech; Greenough prints it after the full stop.

sentences.t:
Tum vero ancipiti mentem formidine pressus
obstipui, steteruntque comae et vox faucibus haesit.
sentences.l:
Then indeed with doubtful in mind dread pressed
I was stunned, and stood up the hair and in the throat the voice stuck.
sentences.i: Then indeed, my mind weighed down by a double dread, I froze; my hair rose, and my voice clung fast in my throat.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Tum vero' is 'then indeed', an intensifier. 'ancipiti… formidine' is an ablative of means, 'by a double fear' ('anceps' means 'two-headed, two-sided'): fear pulling in two ways. 'mentem… pressus' is a perfect passive participle with an accusative of respect, 'pressed in respect of the mind' (a Greek construction that you'll see again, with 'solutae crinem'). 'obstipui' is the perfect of 'obstipesco', 'I was stunned'. 'steteruntque' is the perfect of 'sto' ('stood on end') with '-que', its penultimate syllable short in verse; 'comae' is the nominative plural. 'faucibus' is an ablative of place and 'haesit' the perfect of 'haereo'. The same line comes at II.774, when Creusa's ghost appears.

sentences.t:
Hunc Polydorum auri quondam cum pondere magno
infelix Priamus furtim mandarat alendum
Threicio regi,
sentences.l:
This Polydorus, with of gold once weight great,
unhappy Priam secretly had entrusted to be reared
to the Thracian king,
sentences.i: Poor Priam had once secretly entrusted this Polydorus, together with a great weight of gold, to the Thracian king to be raised,
sentences.n: Aeneas explains the ghost with a flashback, and so the pluperfect. 'mandarat' is 'mandaverat' with the 'v' dropped (a contracted pluperfect, you'll see this constantly). 'alendum' is a gerundive agreeing with 'Polydorum', 'to be reared', expressing purpose after 'mando'. 'furtim' is 'secretly'; 'infelix' is 'ill-fated'. 'auri… cum pondere magno' is 'with a great weight of gold', the genitive 'auri' set before 'cum'. 'Threicio regi' is a dative, the king of Thrace, whom tradition names Polymestor (Virgil does not give his name).

sentences.t:
cum iam diffideret armis
Dardaniae, cingique urbem obsidione videret.
sentences.l:
when now he was losing confidence in the arms
of Dardania, and to be girdled the city with siege he saw.
sentences.i: when he was losing faith in the arms of Dardania and saw the city being ringed with a siege.
sentences.n: 'cum' with the imperfect subjunctives 'diffideret' and 'videret' gives the circumstances ('when', 'since'). 'diffideret' takes a dative, 'armis', 'distrust the arms'. 'Dardaniae' is a genitive with 'armis', 'of Dardania', the Trojan land. 'cingi' is a passive infinitive of 'cingo' after 'videret', so 'urbem' is its subject accusative, 'saw the city being surrounded'; 'obsidione' is an ablative of means.

sentences.i: When the resources of the Trojans were shattered and Fortune had gone from them, he threw in his lot with Agamemnon's cause and the conquering arms, and broke through every bond of right;
sentences.n: 'ille' is the Thracian king. 'ut' is temporal, 'when', with the perfect 'recessit'; 'opes fractae' needs a 'sunt' understood. 'Teucrum' is a genitive plural in -um for 'Teucrorum' (you'll see this constantly), 'of the Trojans'. 'res Agamemnonias' is 'Agamemnon's cause' (an adjective in place of the genitive), and 'victriciaque arma' is 'the victorious arms'. 'secutus' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'sequor', 'having followed', that is, 'siding with'. 'fas omne abrumpit' means that he broke through all that divine law allowed, including the sacred duty to a guest and to a ward. 'abrumpit' is present, as is the next verb, the narrative present.

sentences.t:
Polydorum obtruncat, et auro
vi potitur.
sentences.l:
Polydorus he cuts down, and the gold
by force he gets possession of.
sentences.i: he cuts Polydorus down and takes the gold by force.
sentences.n: 'obtruncat' is 'hacks down, butchers'. 'potitur' is the present of the deponent 'potior', which takes the ablative, here 'auro': 'he gains possession of the gold'. 'vi' is the ablative of 'vis', 'by force'.

sentences.t:
Quid non mortalia pectora cogis,
auri sacra fames?
sentences.l:
What not mortal hearts do you drive,
of gold accursed hunger?
sentences.i: To what deed will you not drive the hearts of mortals, O hunger for gold, thing accursed?
sentences.n: The narrator breaks off to speak to the passion itself (an apostrophe). 'Quid non… cogis' is 'to what do you not drive…': 'quid' stands where prose would have 'ad quid'. 'pectora' is a neuter plural, 'hearts'. 'auri… fames' is 'hunger for gold' (an objective genitive), a vocative; 'sacra' is its adjective, from 'sacer', which can mean both 'holy' and 'devoted to the gods below, accursed'; here 'accursed' is the better sense.

sentences.t:
Postquam pavor ossa reliquit,
delectos populi ad proceres primumque parentem
monstra deum refero, et quae sit sententia posco.
sentences.l:
After the terror left my bones,
the chosen of the people to the leaders and first my father
the portents of the gods I report, and what the opinion be I ask.
sentences.i: When the terror had left my bones, I report the gods' portents to the chosen leaders of the people, and first of all to my father, and ask what they think should be done.
sentences.n: 'Postquam' takes the perfect 'reliquit' (a figure for fear leaving the bones). 'delectos populi… proceres' are 'the chosen chiefs of the people', 'populi' a genitive; 'primum' is an adverb, 'first', going with 'parentem', Anchises. 'monstra deum' has 'deum', the genitive plural in -um for 'deorum' (you'll see this constantly). 'refero' is 'I report'. 'quae sit sententia' is an indirect question, so 'sit' is subjunctive: 'what the opinion is'. 'posco' is 'ask for, demand'.

sentences.t:
Omnibus idem animus, scelerata excedere terra,
linqui pollutum hospitium, et dare classibus austros.
sentences.l:
To all the same mind, from the wicked land to depart,
to be left the polluted hospitality, and to give to the fleets the south winds.
sentences.i: All are of one mind: to quit the guilty land, to abandon a hospitality that has been defiled, and to let the fleet have the south winds.
sentences.n: 'Omnibus idem animus' is a dative of possession with 'est' left out, 'all have the same mind'. The infinitives 'excedere', 'linqui' and 'dare' explain what that mind is. 'scelerata… terra' is an ablative of separation with 'excedere', 'the land defiled by crime'. 'linqui' is the passive infinitive of 'linquo'. 'pollutum hospitium' is 'the guest-friendship that has been polluted', that is, the place where hospitality was broken. 'dare classibus austros' is 'to give the south winds to the fleets', to set sail before them ('austros' is a plural for the south wind, 'classibus' a dative).

sentences.t:
Ergo instauramus Polydoro funus, et ingens
aggeritur tumulo tellus;
sentences.l:
Therefore we renew for Polydorus the funeral, and huge
is heaped up on the mound earth;
sentences.i: So we perform the funeral rites over again for Polydorus, and a great heap of earth is piled upon the mound;
sentences.n: 'instauramus' is 'we renew, repeat', the verb used of performing a rite afresh. 'Polydoro' is a dative of interest. 'funus' is 'funeral rites'. 'aggeritur' is the present passive of 'aggero', 'is heaped up', and 'ingens… tellus' is its subject, 'a vast quantity of earth'; 'tumulo' is a dative with the compound verb, 'heaped on to the mound'.

sentences.i: altars stand for the Shades, mournful with dark blue fillets and black with cypress, and around them the Trojan women with their hair unbound as custom requires;
sentences.n: 'Manibus' is a dative: the Manes are the spirits of the dead (the edition prints the word with a capital). 'stant… arae' is 'altars stand'. 'caeruleis… vittis' is an ablative of means, 'with dark-blue fillets', and 'atra cupresso' is 'black with cypress': the cypress was a tree of mourning, and dark colours belonged to rites for the dead. 'maestae' agrees with 'arae'. 'Iliades' is a Greek feminine plural, 'women of Ilium', in the nominative; 'crinem… solutae' is a perfect passive participle with an accusative of respect, 'loosed as to the hair' (as with 'mentem… pressus' above). 'de more' is 'according to custom'; 'circum' is an adverb.

sentences.t:
inferimus tepido spumantia cymbia lacte
sanguinis et sacri pateras, animamque sepulchro
condimus, et magna supremum voce ciemus.
sentences.l:
we bring in cups foaming with warm milk
and of sacred blood bowls, and the spirit in the tomb
we lay to rest, and with a great voice a last time we call.
sentences.i: We carry to the tomb cups foaming with warm milk and bowls of sacred blood, and lay his spirit to rest in the grave, and call on him one last time in a great voice.
sentences.n: 'inferimus' is 'we bring in', the word for bringing offerings to the dead. 'tepido spumantia… lacte' is 'foaming with warm milk', and 'cymbia' are boat-shaped cups. 'sanguinis et sacri pateras' has 'sacri' agreeing with 'sanguinis', 'bowls of sacred blood'. 'animam… condimus' is 'we lay the spirit to rest'; 'sepulchro' is an ablative of place (the Latin Library prints 'sepulcro': spelling only). 'supremum' is an adverbial accusative, 'for the last time'. 'ciemus' is 'we call out', the last call to the dead.

sentences.t:
Inde, ubi prima fides pelago, placataque venti
dant maria et lenis crepitans vocat Auster in altum,
deducunt socii navis et litora complent:
sentences.l:
Then, when first trust to the sea, and calmed the winds
give the seas and gentle rustling calls the South wind to the deep,
launch the companions the ships and the shores fill:
sentences.i: Then, as soon as the sea can first be trusted, and the winds grant calmed waters, and a gently rustling south wind calls us out to the deep, my comrades haul the ships down and crowd the shores:
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'ubi prima fides pelago' leaves out 'est': 'when there is first trust for the sea', that is, when the sea first becomes reliable. 'placata' agrees with 'maria': 'the winds give the seas calmed'. 'lenis crepitans… Auster' is 'a gentle, rustling south wind'. 'deducunt… navis' is the technical word for launching ships ('navis' an accusative plural in -is), and 'socii', 'comrades', is the subject, put after the clauses that lead to it. 'litora complent' is 'fill the shores', with the bustle of embarking.

sentences.t: provehimur portu, terraeque urbesque recedunt.
sentences.l: we are carried forward from the harbour, and lands and cities recede.
sentences.i: We stand out from the harbour, and lands and cities slip away behind us.
sentences.n: 'provehimur' is the present passive of 'proveho', 'we are carried forward', here 'we put out to sea'. 'portu' is an ablative of separation. 'terraeque urbesque' is the double '-que', 'both lands and cities', and 'recedunt' is 'draw back, fall away'.

sentences.t:
Sacra mari colitur medio gratissima tellus
Nereidum matri et Neptuno Aegaeo,
sentences.l:
Sacred in the middle of the sea is cultivated, most pleasing, a land
to the Nereids' mother and to Aegean Neptune,
sentences.i: In the midst of the sea lies a holy land, dearest to the mother of the Nereids and to Aegean Neptune,
sentences.n: The island is Delos, though the name does not occur in these lines. 'colitur' is 'is inhabited, honoured'. 'mari… medio' is an ablative of place, 'in the middle of the sea'. 'sacra' and 'gratissima' both agree with 'tellus'; 'gratissima' is a superlative that takes a dative, 'most welcome to'. 'Nereidum matri' is Doris, mother of the Nereids (sea nymphs), and 'Nereidum' is a Greek-style genitive plural in -um. 'Neptuno Aegaeo' is 'to Aegean Neptune', the god of the Aegean.

sentences.t:
quam pius arquitenens oras et litora circum
errantem Mycono e celsa Gyaroque revinxit,
immotamque coli dedit et contemnere ventos.
sentences.l:
which the pious bow-bearer shores and coasts around
wandering, from lofty Myconos and Gyaros bound back,
and unmoved to be inhabited gave and to scorn the winds.
sentences.i: the island which the dutiful Archer, finding it drifting around shores and coasts, bound fast to lofty Myconos and Gyaros, giving it to be lived on, unshaken, and to scorn the winds.
sentences.n: 'quam' is an ordinary relative with 'tellus' as its antecedent. 'pius arquitenens' is Apollo, 'the bow-holder'; 'pius' is 'dutiful, kindly'. 'oras et litora circum' has 'circum' placed after its nouns; 'errantem' agrees with 'quam': in the old story Delos was a floating island. 'Mycono e celsa Gyaroque revinxit' has the preposition 'e' (the form of 'ex' before a consonant) placed after its noun 'Mycono' and before the adjective 'celsa', which agrees with it; 'Gyaroque' is the second ablative. Literally the island is 'bound back from lofty Myconos and Gyaros': 'ex' with a verb of binding can mean 'fastened on, hanging from', so the sense is 'bound fast to' its two neighbours, and it no longer drifts. 'immotam… dedit coli et contemnere ventos' is 'gave it to be inhabited and to scorn the winds', 'dedit' with a passive infinitive and an active one.

sentences.t: Huc feror;
sentences.l: Hither I am borne;
sentences.i: Here I am carried;
sentences.n: 'feror' is the present passive of 'fero', as at 11 and 16; 'huc' is 'hither'. The narrative present moves quickly to the landing.

sentences.t:
haec fessos tuto placidissima portu
accipit:
sentences.l:
this the weary in a safe harbour most calm
receives:
sentences.i: this island, most peaceful, takes us in, worn out as we are, within a safe harbour:
sentences.n: 'haec' is the island, the subject of 'accipit'. 'fessos' is an accusative plural, 'us, the weary', the object. 'tuto… portu' is an ablative of place, 'in a safe harbour', and 'placidissima' is a superlative agreeing with 'haec', 'most calm'. The colon introduces what they do on landing.

sentences.t: egressi veneramur Apollinis urbem.
sentences.l: having disembarked we revere Apollo's city.
sentences.i: Landing, we pay reverence to the city of Apollo.
sentences.n: 'egressi' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'egredior', 'having gone ashore'. 'veneramur' is the present of the deponent 'veneror', 'we worship'. 'Apollinis urbem' is Apollo's city on Delos (Apollo was born on the island).

sentences.i: King Anius, who is king of men and priest of Phoebus as well, his temples bound with fillets and sacred laurel, comes to meet us;
sentences.n: 'Anius' is the legendary king and priest of Delos (in the tradition a son of Apollo). 'rex idem hominum Phoebique sacerdos' means 'king of men and also (idem) priest of Phoebus', 'hominum' and 'Phoebi' being genitives. 'redimitus tempora' is the perfect passive participle of 'redimio' with an accusative of respect, 'bound as to the temples' (the same construction as 'pressus mentem' above). 'vittis et sacra… lauro' are ablatives of means, with 'sacra' agreeing with 'lauro', 'sacred laurel', the tree of Apollo. 'occurrit' is 'comes to meet' (present; the perfect has the same form).

sentences.t: veterem Anchisen adgnovit amicum.
sentences.l: the old Anchises he recognized as a friend.
sentences.i: he recognized Anchises as an old friend.
sentences.n: 'Anchisen' is the Greek accusative singular in -en (you'll see this constantly with Greek names). 'adgnovit' is the perfect of 'adgnosco', 'recognize' (Greenough's spelling; the Latin Library prints 'agnouit'). 'veterem… amicum' is a predicative accusative, 'as an old friend'.

sentences.t: Iungimus hospitio dextras, et tecta subimus.
sentences.l: We join in hospitality right hands, and the roofs we go under.
sentences.i: We clasp hands in welcome and enter beneath his roof.
sentences.n: 'Iungimus… dextras' is 'we join right hands', the clasp of friendship; 'hospitio' is 'in hospitality' (an ablative of manner or circumstance). 'tecta' is a neuter plural, 'roofs, the house', and 'subimus' is 'we go under'.

sentences.t: Templa dei saxo venerabar structa vetusto:
sentences.l: The god's temple, built of stone ancient, I was revering:
sentences.i: I did homage to the god's temple, built of age-old stone:
sentences.n: A new paragraph, leading to the prayer. 'Templa' is a plural for the singular, 'the temple'. 'dei' is a genitive, 'of the god', Apollo. 'structa' is the perfect participle of 'struo', 'built', and 'saxo… vetusto' an ablative of material. 'venerabar' is the imperfect of the deponent 'veneror', 'I was worshipping'. The colon introduces the prayer that follows.

sentences.t: “Da propriam, Thymbraee, domum;
sentences.l: “Give our own, Thymbraean, home;
sentences.i: “Give us a home of our own, Thymbraean god;
sentences.n: Aeneas' prayer begins, with the opening “. 'Da' is the imperative of 'do'; the prayer is built on a series of imperatives ('da… da… serva… da'). 'propriam' is 'our own, lasting'. 'Thymbraee' is the vocative of 'Thymbraeus', a title of Apollo from Thymbra, a plain near Troy where he had a temple. 'domum' is an accusative, 'home'.

sentences.t:
da moenia fessis
et genus et mansuram urbem;
sentences.l:
give walls to the weary
and a race and a lasting city;
sentences.i: give walls to us who are worn out, and descendants, and a city that will endure;
sentences.n: 'fessis' is a dative, 'to the weary (us)'. 'et genus et mansuram urbem' has the double 'et… et', 'both a race and a lasting city'; 'genus' is 'offspring, posterity'. 'mansuram' is the future active participle of 'maneo', 'about to remain', that is, 'enduring'.

sentences.t:
serva altera Troiae
Pergama, reliquias Danaum atque immitis Achilli.
sentences.l:
preserve a second Troy's
Pergamum, the remnants of the Danaans and of the pitiless Achilles.
sentences.i: preserve a second Pergamum of Troy, and the remnant left by the Greeks and by fierce Achilles.
sentences.n: 'serva' is an imperative, 'save, keep'. 'altera Troiae Pergama' is 'a second Pergamum of Troy' ('Pergama' is the neuter plural, the citadel of Troy, standing for the whole city). 'reliquias' is a second object of 'serva', 'the remnants (that the Greeks and Achilles have left)'. 'Danaum' is a genitive plural in -um for 'Danaorum' (you'll see this constantly), and 'Achilli' is the genitive of 'Achilles' in its Latin-Greek form in -i; 'immitis' is the genitive of 'immitis', 'pitiless'.

sentences.t: Quem sequimur?
sentences.l: Whom do we follow?
sentences.i: Whom are we to follow?
sentences.n: Three short questions follow in quick succession: whom to follow, where to go, where to settle. 'Quem' is an accusative, the object of 'sequimur'.

sentences.t: Quove ire iubes?
sentences.l: Or whither to go do you bid?
sentences.i: Or where do you bid us go?
sentences.n: 'Quove' is 'quo' (to what place) with the enclitic '-ve', 'or'. 'ire' is an infinitive after 'iubes', the accusative 'nos' being understood.

sentences.t: Ubi ponere sedes?
sentences.l: Where to place seats?
sentences.i: Where are we to set up our homes?
sentences.n: A fragment: 'iubes' is carried over from the last question, so 'where (do you bid us) to place our seats?'. 'ponere' is 'to set, found', and 'sedes' is an accusative plural, 'seats, dwellings'.

sentences.t: Da, pater, augurium, atque animis inlabere nostris.”
sentences.l: Give, father, an augury, and into our minds glide.”
sentences.i: Grant a sign, Father, and glide into our minds.”
sentences.n: 'pater' is a vocative, a title given to a god. 'augurium' is 'a sign', the object of 'da'. 'inlabere' is the imperative of the deponent 'inlabor' (Greenough's spelling; the verb is 'illabor'), second person singular, 'glide into'; 'animis… nostris' is a dative with the compound verb. The closing ” ends the prayer.

sentences.t: Vix ea fatus eram:
sentences.l: Hardly these things having said I was:
sentences.i: Hardly had I spoken so:
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'fatus eram' is the pluperfect of the deponent 'for', 'fari', 'I had spoken', with 'ea' the neuter plural 'these things'. The colon introduces what followed.

sentences.t:
tremere omnia visa repente,
liminaque laurusque dei, totusque moveri
mons circum, et mugire adytis cortina reclusis.
sentences.l:
to tremble all things seemed suddenly,
both the thresholds and the laurels of the god, and the whole to move
mountain round, and to bellow in the shrine opened the tripod.
sentences.i: all things seemed suddenly to shake, the threshold and laurels of the god, and the whole mountain round about to stir, and the tripod to bellow in the opened shrine.
sentences.n: 'visa' is a perfect passive participle (with 'sunt' understood) used personally, 'omnia visa' = 'all things seemed', followed by the infinitives 'tremere', 'moveri' and 'mugire', 'to tremble, to be moved, to bellow'. 'liminaque laurusque dei' (with its double '-que') names what shook, as a detail of 'omnia': 'laurus' is a nominative plural of the feminine fourth-declension noun; the laurel was Apollo's tree. 'totusque… mons circum' is 'the whole mountain round about'. 'cortina' is the cauldron, the tripod of the oracle. 'adytis… reclusis' is an ablative absolute: 'adytum' is the inner shrine, here 'thrown open'.

sentences.t: Submissi petimus terram, et vox fertur ad auris:
sentences.l: Humbled we seek the ground, and a voice is borne to the ears:
sentences.i: We bow down to the earth, and a voice comes to our ears:
sentences.n: 'Submissi' is 'lowered, humbled' (the Latin Library prints 'summissi'; spelling only). 'petimus terram' is 'we make for the ground', that is, we throw ourselves down. 'vox fertur ad auris' repeats the wording of 40, again for a voice from beyond; 'auris' is an accusative plural in -is. The colon introduces the oracle.

sentences.t:
“Dardanidae duri, quae vos a stirpe parentum
prima tulit tellus, eadem vos ubere laeto
accipiet reduces.
sentences.l:
“Hardy Dardanids, which you from the stock of parents
first bore, land, the same you with fertile breast
will receive returning.
sentences.i: “Hardy sons of Dardanus, the land that first bore you from your fathers' stock will welcome you back, on your return, to her rich breast.
sentences.n: The god's speech begins, with the opening “; the speaker is Apollo, though the text does not say so. 'Dardanidae' is a vocative plural, 'descendants of Dardanus', the founder of the Trojan line; 'duri' means 'hardy, tough'. 'quae… prima tulit tellus' is a relative clause before its antecedent: the antecedent 'tellus' is taken up by 'eadem', 'the same land'. 'a stirpe parentum' is 'from the stock of your parents, ancestors'. 'ubere laeto' is an ablative of manner, 'with a fruitful breast' (a mother's breast, a land's richness). 'accipiet' is future, and 'reduces' a predicative nominative plural, 'as returning ones'. The oracle does not name the land, and Anchises will misread it.

sentences.t: Antiquam exquirite matrem:
sentences.l: The ancient mother seek out:
sentences.i: Seek out your ancient mother:
sentences.n: 'exquirite' is a plural imperative of 'exquiro'. 'antiquam matrem' is 'the ancient mother', the ancestral land, a metaphor taken up from 'parentum' and 'ubere'. The colon introduces the answer in the next line.

sentences.t:
hic domus Aeneae cunctis dominabitur oris,
et nati natorum, et qui nascentur ab illis.”
sentences.l:
here the house of Aeneas over all shores will rule,
and the sons of sons, and those who will be born from them.”
sentences.i: There the house of Aeneas shall hold mastery over every shore, with his sons' sons and those who are born of them in turn.”
sentences.n: 'hic' is an adverb, 'here, in that land'. 'domus Aeneae' is 'the house, the dynasty of Aeneas'. 'dominabitur' is the future of the deponent 'dominor', which takes the dative 'cunctis… oris', 'over all shores'. 'nati natorum' is 'children of children', 'et qui nascentur ab illis' 'and those who will be born of them' ('nascentur' is the future of the deponent 'nascor'). Virgil is here rewriting a prophecy made in the Iliad (Book XX), where Poseidon says that the might of Aeneas will rule the Trojans, and his sons' sons after him; Virgil enlarges it to 'all shores'. The closing ” ends the oracle.
